(CNN) -- Polygamist sect leader Warren Jeffs tried to hang himself earlier this year while he was in jail awaiting trial, according to court documents unsealed by a Utah judge on Tuesday. Sect leader Warren Jeffs arrives in court to hear the verdict against him September 25 in St. George, Utah. Jeffs, the leader and so-called prophet of the 10,000-member Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints, is now awaiting sentencing after being convicted on two counts of being an accomplice to rape. The documents, released by Fifth District Judge James Shumate at the request of the media, also indicate that Jeffs confessed to "immorality" with a "sister" and a daughter more than 30 years ago. Among the documents is a competency report on Jeffs completed in April, in which social worker Eric Nielsen wrote that throughout the month of January, Jeffs refused food and drink and developed ulcers on his knees from kneeling in prayer for hours. On January 28, the report said, he attempted to hang himself in his cell. In the days following the suicide attempt, while he was on suicide watch, Jeffs on separate occasions threw himself against the wall and banged his head on the wall. Jail transcripts show that Jeffs' suicide attempt came three days after a visit with his brother, Nephi, in which he said, "I am not the prophet. I never was the prophet, and I have been deceived by the powers of evil ... I ask for everyone's forgiveness." Jeffs also told his brother: "Farewell forever." The day before that, Jeffs told a follower in a phone conversation that he was "covered with immorality with a sister and a daughter when I was younger." In the FLDS, members call adult women "sister," and Jeffs' meaning was unclear. Jeffs' defense attorneys, who argued against the release of the documents, said in a motion opposing the unsealing of the statements that Jeffs recanted them the following month. Defense attorneys claim Jeffs' medical condition influenced his state of mind when the statements were made. They presented Shumate with a letter from another Jeffs attorney, arguing that the statements' release could influence an Arizona jury when Jeffs stands trial in that state. Jeffs, 51, was convicted in September of being an accomplice to rape. He was accused of using his religious influence over his followers to coerce a 14-year-old girl into marriage to her 19-year-old cousin. He faces a sentence of up to life in prison when he is sentenced November 20. The FLDS -- which is not affiliated with the mainstream Mormon church -- is based in the side-by-side border towns of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona. Jeffs, a former school headmaster, is the son of the sect's previous president and "prophet," Rulon Jeffs, who died in 2002. Jeffs was on the FBI's 10 most wanted fugitives list when he was arrested in August 2006 outside Las Vegas, Nevada. Critics say that inside the FLDS, marriages are arranged for girls as young as 13, and competition for brides may be reduced by exiling male teens and young men. If male followers are excommunicated, critics claim, wives and children can be reassigned. During Jeffs' trial, defense attorneys claimed authorities were persecuting Jeffs because of his religious beliefs, including practicing polygamy as the way to heaven. If Jeffs disavowed being the prophet of the FLDS, it could cause upheaval within the secretive sect. However, two of his followers who spoke to CNN -- although FLDS members usually do not talk to reporters -- said they do not believe he made the statements. "He is a perfectly priestly man," said a woman who identified herself as Cathy. "He is a man of God, and we will always love him. Once a prophet, always a prophet." Her husband, Patrick, told CNN, "It's hogwash. I don't believe it ... I will always consider him my prophet." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Gary Tuchman contributed to this report.

Polygamist sect leader Warren Jeffs attempted suicide in his jail cell earlier this year while awaiting trial, according to court documents unsealed Tuesday by a Utah judge. 

Jeffs—the leader and self-proclaimed prophet of the 10,000-member Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter Day Saints (FLDS)—is currently awaiting sentencing following his conviction in St. George, Utah, on two counts of rape as an accomplice.

Released by Fifth District Judge James Shumate following media requests, the court filings reveal that Jeffs confessed to "immorality" involving a "sister" and a daughter over three decades ago. Among the unsealed records is an April competency evaluation conducted by social worker Eric Nielsen. The report notes that throughout January, Jeffs repeatedly refused food and water, developing severe ulcers on his knees from spending hours in prayer. On January 28, he attempted to hang himself in his cell.

During the days following his suicide attempt, while placed on suicide watch, Jeffs repeatedly self-harmed by throwing himself against the wall and banging his head. Jail transcripts indicate that the suicide attempt occurred just three days after a visitation with his brother, Nephi, during which Jeffs stated: *"I am not the prophet. I never was the prophet, and I have been deceived by the powers of evil... I ask for everyone's forgiveness."* He added, *"Farewell forever."* 

Just one day prior to that visit, Jeffs admitted to a follower during a phone call that he was *"covered with immorality with a sister and a daughter when I was younger."* Within the FLDS, adult female members are routinely referred to as "sisters," rendering the exact nature of his statement ambiguous.

Defense attorneys actively opposed the release of these documents. In a motion resisting the unsealing, they stated that Jeffs recanted the admissions the following month, maintaining that his deteriorated physical condition severely compromised his state of mind at the time. The defense also submitted a letter from another attorney representing Jeffs, arguing that the public disclosure of these statements could unfairly bias a future jury during his upcoming trial in Arizona.

The 51-year-old sect leader was convicted in September for utilizing his religious authority over followers to coerce a 14-year-old girl into marrying her 19-year-old cousin. Facing a potential sentence of up to life in prison, his sentencing is scheduled for November 20. 

The FLDS—which maintains no affiliation with the mainstream Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints—is headquartered in the adjacent border communities of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona. Jeffs, a former school headmaster, assumed control of the organization following the 2002 death of his father, former sect president and prophet Rulon Jeffs. At the time of his arrest near Las Vegas, Nevada, in August 2006, Jeffs was listed on the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list.

Critics of the FLDS contend that the group routinely arranges marriages for girls as young as 13 and systematically exiles teenage boys and young men to reduce competition for brides. Furthermore, critics assert that when male members are excommunicated, their wives and children are reassigned to other men. Throughout the trial, defense attorneys argued that authorities were persecuting Jeffs for his religious convictions, including the belief that practicing polygamy is a prerequisite for entering heaven.

While a public disavowal of Jeffs' prophetic status could trigger severe upheaval within the secretive sect, some adherents remain steadfast. In a rare exception to the group's usual refusal to engage with reporters, two followers expressed complete disbelief regarding the statements. 

"He is a perfectly priestly man," said a member identifying herself as Cathy. "He is a man of God, and we will always love him. Once a prophet, always a prophet." Her husband, Patrick, echoed the sentiment, telling reporters, "It's hogwash. I don't believe it... I will always consider him my prophet."

*(CNN’s Gary Tuchman contributed to this report.)*

In a dramatic unsealing of once-confidential court records and psychological evaluations, a Utah judge—responding to petitions from a coalition of media organizations—has provided the public with an unprecedented look into the dark, turbulent jailhouse life of Warren Jeffs. The documents detail the physical collapse, mental unraveling, and shocking private admissions of the self-proclaimed prophet of the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS) as he awaited trial in 2007 on charges of accomplice to rape.

Far from the stoic, infallible holy man he projected to his thousands of devoted followers, the unsealed evaluations depict a man driven to despair, self-harm, and profound spiritual crisis while held in Washington County, Utah.

### A Mind in Freefall: Fasting and a Suicide Attempt

The released reports reveal that during his pretrial detention, Jeffs descended into extreme isolation and physical deterioration. Believing he was undergoing a supreme spiritual test—or facing punishment from God—Jeffs engaged in severe fasting, losing dozens of pounds and placing his life in danger. 

The psychological reports document a crucial turning point: Jeffs attempted suicide in his jail cell by trying to hang himself with a bedsheet. Corrections officers intervened, saving his life, after which he was placed under 24-hour suicide watch and subjected to intensive medical monitoring. Jail staff noted that Jeffs was frequently found kneeling in prayer for hours on end, suffering from severe sleep deprivation, and exhibiting signs of profound depression and catatonia.

### Renouncing the Prophethood and Admitting Guilt

Perhaps the most damaging disclosures within the competency reports are Jeffs' own words regarding his spiritual standing and past conduct. During psychiatric interviews and monitored phone conversations with close family members, Jeffs explicitly stripped himself of his divine mantle. 

"I am not a prophet," Jeffs repeatedly declared, according to the records. He told evaluators that he was a "wicked man" who had lied to his congregation and usurped a holy calling he was never worthy to hold. 

Even more damning were his specific confessions. Jeffs admitted to evaluators and family that he had engaged in widespread sexual misconduct, including acts involving underage girls and members of his own extended family. He referred to himself as the "greatest sinner on earth," expressing a belief that he was damned and that God had abandoned him for his crimes. For a religious leader whose absolute authority governed every aspect of his followers' lives—from arranged marriages to business ownership—these admissions struck at the very heart of the FLDS theological structure.

### The Defense Strategy: Mental Incompetence

Faced with these damaging revelations, Jeffs' defense attorneys moved aggressively to suppress the reports and stall the criminal proceedings. They argued that their client’s confessions and renunciations were not genuine admissions of guilt, but rather the incoherent ramblings of a man experiencing a catastrophic mental breakdown.

The defense contended that prolonged solitary confinement, extreme malnutrition from fasting, and overwhelming stress had induced a state of psychosis or severe religious mania. They argued that Jeffs was physically and mentally incapacitated, incapable of rational thought, and legally incompetent to assist in his own defense. According to his legal team, his statements were the product of a broken mind trying to rationalize a devastating fall from power, rendering them unreliable for court proceedings.

### Judicial Ruling and Lasting Impact

Despite the defense’s assertions, state-appointed mental health experts who evaluated Jeffs concluded that while he was experiencing extreme psychological distress and religious despair, he retained a functional understanding of the legal charges against him. Evaluators noted that some of his behavior appeared calculated, suggesting he was capable of manipulation despite his fragile state. The judge ultimately ruled that Jeffs was legally competent to stand trial.

The unsealing of these records delivered a permanent blow to Jeffs' image. For years, FLDS leadership had managed to maintain an aura of divine invulnerability around Jeffs, convincing loyalists in the polygamist enclaves of Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona, that his imprisonment was merely a persecution of the righteous. 

The court documents shattered that myth, exposing a man who, behind closed doors, had abandoned his divine claims and confessed to the very crimes his followers insisted were government fabrications. Though Jeffs would later attempt to reassert his control over the church from behind bars, the unsealed records permanently documented the moment the "prophet" broke, revealing the human and moral collapse of one of the nation's most notorious cult leaders.

The thousands of pages of medical logs, recorded jailhouse phone calls, and investigative transcripts—unsealed as part of ongoing legal proceedings related to the Fundamentalist Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints (FLDS)—offer an unprecedented look into the psychological collapse of one of America’s most notorious cult leaders. 

For decades, Jeffs ruled the polygamous sect with an iron fist, commanding total obedience from an estimated 10,000 followers who believed his word was the literal voice of God. But the unsealed documents paint a starkly different picture: a broken man confessing to fraud, suffering from severe medical crises, and trying to end his own life.

### A Suicide Attempt in the Dark

According to jail logs and medical records from early 2007, while Jeffs was being held in Utah awaiting trial on rape accomplice charges, he entered a state of severe self-deprivation. Jeffs engaged in extreme fasting, refusing both food and water for extended periods, which led to a rapid deterioration of his physical and mental health.

The unsealed records detail a critical incident in which correctional officers found Jeffs unresponsive in his cell after he attempted to hang himself using a piece of clothing. 

Medical reports indicate Jeffs suffered severe bodily trauma and was rushed to a local hospital, where he was placed in a medically induced coma. Doctors noted that Jeffs was suffering from extreme dehydration, organ stress, and severe ulcerations. 

"The inmate has demonstrated severe suicidal ideation driven by intense spiritual distress and paranoia," one attending physician wrote in a newly released psychiatric evaluation. "He repeatedly stated that he was 'unworthy to live' and had 'failed God.'"

### 'I am a fake': The Prophet’s Secret Confession

Perhaps the most damaging revelations within the unsealed documents are the transcripts of audio recordings in which Jeffs explicitly renounced his divine authority—a secret his inner circle fought for years to keep from the church faithful.

In a recorded telephone conversation with his brother, Seth Jeffs, and in subsequent statements to investigators, the FLDS leader broke down, weeping as he admitted that his entire ministry was built on falsehoods.

"I am not the prophet. I am a wicked man," Jeffs said, according to a transcript of a January 2007 recording. "I have lied to the people. I have committed great sins... God has rejected me."

In another transcript, Jeffs is recorded telling family members that he had usurped power following the death of his father, Rulon Jeffs, in 2002. "I am a fake," Jeffs confessed. "I was never called of God. Everything I did was of my own pride."

Legal experts say these confessions were likely driven by a combination of severe psychological pressure, physical exhaustion from forced fasting, and the looming reality of spending the rest of his life behind bars. Jeffs was later convicted in Texas in 2011 on two counts of child sexual assault related to taking underage "spiritual wives" and sentenced to life plus 20 years.

### Fractures, Denial, and Cognitive Dissonance

The unsealing of these records has sent shockwaves through the splintered communities of the FLDS, located primarily along the Utah-Arizona border in Short Creek (Hildale, Utah, and Colorado City, Arizona), as well as remote compounds in Texas, South Dakota, and Canada.

For former members who escaped the cult, the documents provide a painful form of vindication.

"We were taught that Warren Jeffs was higher than Jesus Christ, that he was incapable of sin, and that his words were scripture," said Elissa Wall, a former FLDS member whose testimony helped convict Jeffs in 2007. "To read his own words admitting he lied to us—it’s devastating for those of us who lost our childhoods to him, but it is also the ultimate proof that we were held captive by a fraud."

However, among Jeffs’ remaining loyalists, the reaction has been marked by deep cognitive dissonance and fierce denial. 

Sources familiar with the isolated community say that church elders—who still enforce Jeffs’ decrees from his maximum-security prison cell in Palestine, Texas—have moved quickly to suppress the unsealed records. Followers are reportedly being told that the transcripts are government fabrications, created using artificial technology or psychological torture to destroy their faith.

"When a cult leader’s disavowal is revealed, the true believers rarely just pack up and leave," explained Dr. Janja Lalich, a sociologist and expert on cults and coercion. "They resort to mental gymnastics. They will rationalize that Warren was being tested by God like Job, or that he was forced by evil forces to say those things to test the faith of his followers. The cognitive dissonance is too overwhelming for them to accept that their entire worldview is based on a lie."

### An Empire in Ruin

Despite his imprisonment and the revelations of his secret breakdown, Jeffs has continued to exert influence over a shrinking, highly secretive core of followers. In recent years, he has issued increasingly apocalyptic edicts from prison, ordering followers to cease procreation, abandon their homes, and prepare for the end of the world.

Yet, the unsealing of these documents comes at a time when the FLDS church is largely in collapse. Much of the property once owned by the church's communal trust has been redistributed by court-appointed legal administrators, and hundreds of former members have returned to live in the former cult strongholds.

For those who have left, the unsealed records represent the final, tragic chapter of a man who claimed to hold the keys to heaven, but left a legacy of earthly devastation.

"The tragedy isn't just that Warren Jeffs tried to end his life or admitted he was a fraud," said Sam Brower, a private investigator who spent years exposing the FLDS. "The tragedy is the thousands of lives he ruined before he finally confessed the truth to himself."
